en: Preface to the *Anthology of the Chan School’s Citations of Ancient Cases* (Zongmen Niangu Huyi): De Shan said, "In our school, there are no words or phrases; truly, not a single dharma is given to others.

The Old Gautama also said, "In forty-nine years, I have never uttered a single word. Thus, the Three Baskets, the Twelve Divisions of Scripture, and the seventeen hundred cases—[are all but echoes of this truth].
As for these karmic conditions (*nimita*), from where could they have been obtained? This is something that the entire world finds difficult to discuss or comprehend.
Unless one possesses the correct eye of the forehead and the efficacious talisman behind the elbow, it will not be easy to speak of this principle with such a person.

Now, although it is said that there are no words or phrases, the discourse on "host and guest," "question and answer," "the patched robe," and "millet cakes" pervades the monastic groves; yet it is also said that not a single word has ever been spoken.
The characters, contained within golden cases and jade rollers, shine brilliantly like the sun and stars. How could this be so without some underlying reason? I have heard it said:
"One who speaks well may have words that fill the world, yet commits no verbal transgression. This is like a person who, though using their teeth, lips, and tongue all day long, never harms them.
Thus, even if the Dragon Palace were filled to its rafters with scriptures, and the monks as numerous as clouds and water were to sweat [in their study], [the true essence remains beyond words].
Ox! Previously, I had never encountered a single word or phrase [of this kind], and only then did I realize that there was indeed substance to what Gautama and Deshan said.
Master Hui remarked: "The words carry the profound yet leave no path; the tongue speaks, yet it does not speak.
Is this not precisely what he meant? Since our own school began with the seven steps and the overturning of the banner-pole, its influence has flowed down to China.
Though these complications cover the ground, in reality there is not a single word or character that can hang upon the lips of anyone.
Therefore, the descendants of his lineage vie with one another to raise it up and proclaim it, to seize it and bring it forth.

At the moment when the mallet is raised and the whisk is held upright—like a flash of lightning or a clap of thunder—one exalts and one suppresses, becoming ever more extraordinary as they emerge. All of this is utterly beyond the reach of conceptual thought; it is simply like this.
The divine pearl within the sun possesses a radiance of indeterminate colors; how could those who merely feel about the void or grasp at shadows ever be spoken of as its equal?
Thus, Song De compiled the *Jianxi* collection in the past, and Yu Gulin continued it in later times, titling it *Zongmen Tongyao*.
Their selection of materials was both broad and discerning, each with its own intended purpose. For the reader, this is no less than ascending to the summit of Mount Miaofeng.
It is like gazing upon the empty sky and the vast ocean from atop a mountain; one does not realize its height and distance.

It is also like entering the palace of the Sāgara Dragon King, where rare and wondrous treasures glitter before one's eyes, yet one does not realize that one has come to dwell in a land of great wealth.
Thus, this book alone constitutes a major achievement for our school and is certainly sufficient to be highly praised; how much more so since it has further been compiled and assembled.
Thus it is said. I, Fu, being of dull wit, have excavated my remaining thoughts regarding the diligent application of Jianxi Daowei and Gulin Zhenjie.

I have therefore intermittently selected from the various patriarchs from the Song and Yuan dynasties down to the present day—every single *nian* (gathering), every generation, every distinction, and every inquiry—that is sufficient to open the eyes and minds of the human and celestial realms.
All of these have been gathered and continued herein, totaling forty-five fascicles, titled *Zongmen Nian* (Gleanings from the Patriarchal Gate).
This is an ancient compilation. It is as if, from the Jasper Stairs, one further spreads vermilion sand;
it is like the waters flowing from rivers to the sea, and from the sea converging into Lake Anavatapta, reaching the ultimate state of vast and boundless expanse.
Yet, before the Many-Son Stūpa, at midnight, there was that one great matter of transmission and reception regarding the yellow plum. Apart from this, what would it differ from?
To abandon Mount Jing in search of the Buan jade—this I venture to say is truly one great achievement of our school;
it is certainly no exaggeration. Some might say: "The ancients had their own way of engaging with things; this is merely dregs."
"What is the purpose of these matters? Fú said, "Indeed, these are but the dregs of the ancients. May I present you with one or two of the ancients' refined spirits?
The man, his mouth clamped and tongue tied, withdrew with an abashed face. Alas! The precious moon of purity does not reside on the tip of the finger that points toward it;
yet, were it not for one who perceives the Heavenly Mind through and through, one would remain detached from it.
If one seeks elsewhere at the very tip of the finger, how could one ever succeed?

Should anyone hereafter possess a single eye directed toward this, seeing through and through the origin of every strike and every tap of the ancient masters, they would regard this collection as mere dregs;
what could be more appropriate?
Written on the Double Ninth day of the Jiachen year, the third year of the Kangxi era (1664), by the monk Jingfu, a successor of the lineage from Luling,
at the Dailin Hall.
Preface to the *Compendium of Anecdotes from the Chan School*.
The world claims that this one school of the Chan tradition originated from the "holding up of a flower" at Vulture Peak;

yet they do not realize that as soon as Old Gautama set foot upon the earth, pointing to the ground and pointing to the heavens while proclaiming his own supremacy, he had already driven stakes of entanglement throughout the great trichiliocosm.
It is like a target for an archer: it is no more than three feet high, regardless of whether one pierces the willow or circles around it.
The "Tree-Hand" (Śālavatīputra) was but a young child with a yellow mouth who had only recently learned to shoot at sparrows;

yet he could not restrain his impetuosity and, joining with others to seize clods of wet mud, they vied with one another amidst crowds of thousands and tens of thousands, charging across a hundred paces.

With a great shout, they loosed their aim—how could this have been merely Kāśyapa alone discharging a single branch of thistle and mugwort? For forty-nine years, a multitude of arrows flew in chaotic flight.

The old Gautama could do nothing but dodge east and west; in the end, he was utterly helpless. Fortunately, he managed to preserve his life through a complete stratagem and passed away between the twin trees.
Who would have thought that two thousand years later, the lame-legged Yunmen would suddenly emerge, wishing to strike him with a single blow and feed him to the dogs?
Yet he even feigned this, saying, "It is only for the sake of peace throughout the world. Alas for Gautama! He truly must have been enduring unbearable pain.
It is difficult to unfold; calamity arises from within one’s own household. Yet, since Bodhidharma crossed to the East, the lineage was transmitted through six generations to Caoxi (Huineng).
From him, it branched into two streams via Qingyuan and Nanyue. Within a few generations, these two branches further divided into five schools.

As the followers of these five schools emerged, they were as numerous as those chasing a deer, spreading like stars and arranged like chess pieces, filling the land of China. Who among them did not sing their lofty songs at the foot of Mount Gai? Secretly...
Gripping the curtain within, he returned to Pei, his heart filled with grief. Who could surpass Yunfeng Yue in this regard? Yet I still harbor a slight regret.
I have often said that although Yunmen possessed the path for emerging from himself, he lacked the strategy to settle the chaos.

These words were not intended as "borrowing a sword to kill a man"; rather, they were simply an unwillingness to let the old master Yuan’s single blow go to waste. The world has declined and the Way has become obscure.

Rare are those who seek the Way, and vast is the expanse of time. To whom, then, shall I ultimately entrust this? In the autumn of the Jiachen year, while a guest in Hulin, I was able to meet with the Venerable Master Bairyam Ui-jeung and renew our friendship of twenty years.
We stayed together for two nights by the cold lamp, engaging in lofty discourse spanning the ages, and it was only then that I was first able to submit [my work] for correction:
the *Tongyao* (Essentials of the School Gate). Since the time of Master Goeun, among the patriarchs of the school throughout the land...

The authors [of these works] are as numerous as a forest, yet none have been previously collected. Fearing that they might become scattered and lost, Bairyam searched for them exhaustively and investigated them thoroughly, exerting himself to the utmost until he compiled forty-five volumes.
He entitled this work *Zongmen Niangu Huiji* (Comprehensive Collection of Anecdotes from the Chan School).

Regarded as a grand compendium surpassing the *Tongyao*, it serves as a distant bridge and raft for the Dharma-gate; it can truly be said to have rendered great service in stemming the turbulent waves.

It is a single pillar; yet, one cannot help but feel some concern. Why is this? At a time when the ancestral wind is still in its infancy, everyone claims to be the Lurong Hongzhi when speaking of verses and eulogies, and everyone claims to be the Zhaojue Wansong when speaking of "picking up" [the essence].

Little do they realize that these four elders possessed refined and pure integrity, each excelling in their own particular strengths, whereas those who are called... [the current practitioners] merely circle around...
When the arrow pierces the willow, one who can surpass and outshine the venerable old masters will surely not be entirely without words.

Someone said: "The Precious Mirror of White Rock is displayed before the hall; the beautiful and the ugly distinguish themselves naturally. When the Mo-ya sword is held in hand, how dare the *wangliang* spirits come forward?"
It seems there is no need for those below the dais to watch the proceedings, for they will shed tears for the ancients. Alas!
It is not that I am unaware that Baeryam possesses these two things; were it not for Baeryam, how would I dare to make such a claim?

Those who read this collection will come to know Baeryam’s dedication of heart, which will suffice to allow us to behold the virtues of the former masters in our own day. Thus, will not our Way be greatly honored once more?
I look toward future generations with hope.
Written by the ancestral-lineage śramaṇa Dàchéng at Bànguó Monastery in Húlín, following his stay at Qīxiá Chán Monastery on Mount Shè in Jīnlíng.

**Preface to the *Compendium of Gleanings from the Chan School’s Excerpts and Citations*:** The compilation of this work gathers those one thousand seven hundred cases of karmic conditions (*jiyuan*) that have existed since the time of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

Having been handled by the hands of the masters of our school, each case has been picked up and examined once; it is as if gold were being enhanced in color. Truly, it is capable of making even the most stale and worn-out "wild vines" (*geteng*) suddenly [vibrant].
Strange phenomena then arose. He then began to select and comment upon these sayings with appropriateness, placing particular emphasis on the kōans (ji-yuan).
It is for this reason that he alone was given the title "The Ancestral School’s *Nian-gu* (Selections from the Past)."
This is the collection of the comments and expositions by various masters from the Song and Yuan dynasties onward.

Since those already recorded in the *Tongyao* (Essentials of the Lineage) have been included, all subsequent instances—whether a single comment, a specific distinction, a period-specific exposition, or a formal inquiry—that have not yet been recorded by masters from the Song and Yuan down to the present day, shall follow the established regulations of the *Tongyao* and be appended in their proper sequence.
Furthermore, regarding those masters who possess comments (*nianyu*) for which the *Tongyao* lacks the corresponding karmic occasions (*jinyuan*), [these shall likewise be added].

[Where there were omissions,] these have been supplemented. Regarding the essential points, those that possessed the karmic conditions [for inclusion] but lacked *nianyu* (critical comments) have not been recorded here.

Among the various regional *yulu* (recorded sayings) of past and present, as for those *nianyu* that address critical phrases from other eras, some exist as well-edited single-volume editions currently in circulation;
some are contained within the formal discourses of *shangtang* (ascending the hall) and *xiaocan* (small sermons); and some remain as draft manuscripts yet to be transcribed.

Regarding those who passed through Li and Zhao: for those whose names have vanished without trace, leaving only their deeds and epigraphic records to be examined, I have recorded each one according to the facts, not daring to fabricate anything from thin air.
The remarks of the various masters are all like uncut jade and unrefined gold; how could one bear to cut them away and discard them?
However, beneath each koan, they must be clearly categorized as a single group. Although they are equally Bian-wei (Bianliang’s jade), differences in quality and thickness cannot be avoided.
This is why one cannot help but pay close attention to this selection process. As for those whose phrasing and meaning are identical, they may indeed be called "twin pearls."
It is like two jade discs joined together; yet I dare not preserve them both side by side, fearing that they might lead to mutual plagiarism.
Since the weight of this work has now fallen into the hands of a master craftsman, I dare not fail to follow his impartial judgment regarding what should be included or excluded.
If one can manifest a separate hand and eye beyond this present koan, exercising mastery over killing and giving life at will,

then even if they are a lay practitioner or a white-robed householder, no one would dare disregard them or fail to record their deeds. Conversely, if one merely relies on copying patterns and lacks the skill to transform base iron into gold,
being devoid of the tongs and hammers of vertical and horizontal, bestowing and taking away, then even if they currently occupy a curved-back chair and their fame shakes the common world—
Yan: It is absolutely impossible to follow their partiality and flattery by making a haphazard collection.
The *Shujing* (Book of Documents) speaks of "compiling and gathering"; in principle, one must be comprehensive in what is included.

However, as for those sages and worthies who remain deeply hidden and store their treasures within, compounded by the fact that their lands are remote and their paths distant—their solitary and unique character on those shores makes them unwilling to seek the knowledge of others, and how could others possibly [know them]?

I have exhausted my efforts to understand it all. As for those lofty views and far-reaching insights that I have been unable to investigate thoroughly, may the celestial dragons and nāgas of future generations not fail me, but shall naturally supplement them.

That characters change after being transcribed three times—such as the error of "wu" becoming "ma"—is a phenomenon that has long existed; yet within the essential compendium, there is a profound underlying principle.
Regarding the errors in the citations and the distortions in the recorded sayings, I have consulted various *Denglu* (Lamp Records) and edited them according to the intent of the patriarchs;
every point has been verified for its factual accuracy, ensuring there is no doubt or confusion.

The genealogy of the lamp records is not what this book urgently requires; nevertheless, the sequence of the volumes still follows the chronological divisions of the Southern Peak (Nanyue) and Qingyuan lineages.
This is intended to make it easy for students to consult and verify who was realized through which lineage, so that the conditions of their karmic encounters may naturally become apparent.
For when such karmic encounters are recorded, there must necessarily have been the individuals involved.

Regarding *kōan* (public cases): whenever masters and disciples, or host and guest, meet, one observes their functional expression (*jiryō*) to determine to which lineage they belong and thus where they are categorized.

This is not something that can be arbitrarily shifted from one side to another. For example, Ling Xingpo’s “folding her hands and crying out to the blue heavens” is included within the chapter on Fubei;
likewise, the "three thoughts" of the pancake-selling old woman on the road to Liyang [are included in the relevant case].
If one points to that single mind and collects it within the chapter on Deshan, then it would be difficult to account for the cases of Fubei and Deshan.

Furthermore, regarding the single phrase concerning "the arising and ceasing never ceasing" from Luoshan’s question to Shishuang and Yantou, which is recorded in the chapter on Luoshan, one clearly sees that there is a source for his realization; yet, when discussing the function of responding to students, [it is not limited to that].
Furthermore, it would be more appropriate to include this within the section on Yantou.
If one understands this, the investigation of *gong'an* will naturally not require further deliberation.

△ When the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, the seventh of the Seven Buddhas, first descended into birth, he pointed one hand toward heaven and one hand toward earth,
walked seven steps, and gazed in the four directions, saying: "In the heavens above and the earth below, I alone am the Honored One."
Yunmen Wenyan said, "Had I seen him at that time, I would have struck him dead with a single blow and fed him to the dogs, so as to ensure peace throughout the world.
Xuedou Xian said, "I would have immediately overturned the meditation seat!"
Fayan Yi said, "Yunmen’s aura and momentum are truly immense, yet fundamentally he lacks the principles of the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, an elder remarked, "I thought there was no one to provide such testimony. Xuedou said, "The hook is set in a place beyond doubt."
Langya Jue said, "Yunmen may truly be said to 'offer this profound mind to serve every dust mote and land'; this is what is called repaying the Buddha's kindness.
Yunfeng Yue said, "Although Yunmen possesses a strategy for settling chaos, he lacks the way to emerge from it himself."
Fachang Yu said: "Yunmen’s 'A fine blow' is too late. Before he has even left the Tuṣita Heaven, one should give him a hammer-blow right under his heels.
Nevertheless, it is still like drawing a bow after the thief has fled."
Letan Ying said: "Śākyamuni was as if he were alone in the world.
Had he encountered a monk with clear eyes at that time, he would have had no way to ascend to heaven and no door to enter the earth.
Nevertheless, even so, it must be like filling a bronze sand-pan with oil before one can succeed."
Tiantong Hua said: "Although Yunmen’s story has been widely circulated, it cannot avoid falling into another's pitfall.
Gaofeng Miao said: "The World-Honored One was much like a sacred tortoise dragging its tail; he brought about the very omen of his own destruction.
Although Yunmen fully upheld the orthodox command, he too was merely increasing ignorance for the sake of others' idle affairs. At that time, one should simply...
Draw a circle on the ground and write the character "ding" (丁) within it; then extend both hands to show it.
One can take it for granted that [the opponent] will melt away like ice and crumble like a fortress.

When heaven and earth were opened up, it was he who possessed the skillful hand. Although Yunmen may have considered righteousness when seeing profit, tell me:

can a single blow of the staff truly strike him dead? True understanding does not depend on a thousand cups of wine; a single cup of clear tea can also intoxicate a person. [Suddenly] picking up his staff, he said:
"Are there any among you who were born together and will die together? For now, step aside.

But how so? Although Yunmen had a way to emerge, he lacked the means to settle the chaos."
Regarding this plot, he further said: "If Shouchang had been there at that time, even if the Yellow-faced Gautama were to speak thus, one should simply step forward, join one's palms, and say:

"Why is this? It is because when the Way prevails in the world, the common people do not engage in idle debate.

After a long pause, he brushed [the whisk] once and said: "I serve only the One, who is noble as Heaven and Earth; let the various paths follow their own respective authorities."

Is there anyone here who does not consent? Come forward! I wish to ask you: what is that single penetration?"
Yungai’s original text says: “The World-Honored One summoned thus; the one with five supernatural powers responded thus.
What is this one power? After a long silence, he said: “The beautiful maiden has already returned to the celestial void; the foolish lad still crouches by the fire.”

they often mistake the zero-point on the scale at a single location.

"That one shout—everyone has yet to even dream of it. Ancient Nanmen said:

when the World-Honored One was squeezed by the immortal, he had no way to turn his body; he could only take the wrong for the right. If it were this mountain monk, as soon as—"

Zong. One day, the World-Honored One ascended the seat and sat in silence. Ānanda struck the gavel and said, "I request the World-Honored One to preach the Dharma.

"Just now, because those two bhikṣus had committed an offense against the Vinaya, they have now been sent away. Why does the World-Honored One not preach the Dharma?"

Is there anyone who could have dodged it?"

"Yet one sees my Dharma-body.

"Where have you gone? One woman asked, "What? What? As the other women gazed intently, each attained realization.

The woman said, "In my home, the four requisites and the seven treasures are all fully provided; I require only three things: first, a single trunk of a rootless tree;
second, a patch of ground where neither sun nor shade exists; and third, a mountain valley that does not echo when called.
Śakra said, "Of everything else you require, I have it all; as for these three things, I truly do not possess them."
“Yes,” the woman replied. “If you did not possess this, how could you save others? Śakra was at a loss for words; he then went with her to inform the World-Honored One.

"You have not brought shame upon the Holy Woman.

"Jiuliuguanjiu! Jiuliuguanjiu! Even so, one cannot yet avoid the laughter of bystanders. Baoshou then said:
"The World-Honored One has not forgotten his past practices; the elder merely responded to the occasion as a matter of form.
Both must be set aside to one side. As for the devas scattering flowers and offering praise—tell me, was there benefit or harm in it?"
Let those possessed of the eye examine and discern this for themselves.
As the World-Honored One was walking together with Ānanda, he saw an ancient stūpa of a Buddha. The World-Honored One then paid homage to it.
Ānanda asked, "Whose stūpa is this? The World-Honored One replied, "It is the stūpa of past Buddhas. Ānanda said, "The past Buddhas..."
"Whose disciple is the Buddha? The World-Honored One replied, "He is my disciple. Ānanda said, "It should be so.
Tiantong Wu said: "If I were Ānanda, when the World-Honored One said, 'He is my disciple,' I would simply ask—"
"What kind of disciple is this Buddha? Waiting for the World-Honored One to open his mouth, he immediately prostrates and departs;
this is groundless. Yet he claims it 'should be thus. To turn the rudder against the wind—how can this be the act of a true man?"
The heavens gather thick clouds; the World-Honored One speaks with an echo from within. Ānanda hides his blade within his words—he too deserves a beating.
Why is this so? As a model for gods and humans, one must not employ mechanical artifice.
Lianfu Ce said: "Ānanda was not clever. At that time, seeing that he was my disciple, why did he not immediately prostrate three times?
This would have left the Yellow-Faced Old Man with nowhere to stand."
On the day of the *pravāraṇā*, because Mañjuśrī had spent the summer retreat in three different places, Kāśyapa intended to strike the gavel to expel him.
As soon as he raised the gavel, he saw hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Mañjuśrīs. Kāśyapa exhausted all his supernatural powers, yet he could not lift the gavel.
The World-Honored One then asked Kāśyapa, "Which Mañjuśrī do you intend to expel? Kāśyapa was speechless.
Zhaojue Qin said, "It is a pity he let it pass. At that time, had I waited for Old Śākyamuni to say, 'Which Mañjuśrī do you intend to expel?
I would have struck him with a blow. Let us see how he would have met his match. Yunju Yuan said, "When one house has trouble, a hundred houses are busy."
Tiantong Jue said: "The golden-colored dhūta had heart but no gallantry. At that time, he should have carried out the order completely;
do not say that even hundreds of thousands of millions of Mañjuśrīs would have been spared—this very Gautama of the yellow face would have been expelled as well.

Not only did this establish the true wind standing like a wall, but it also caused later generations to know that in our gate of patch-robed monks, there is no place for you idle Buddhas or idle Bodhisattvas."
The Patriarch could not.
Baoning Miao said, "The Great and Small Kāśyapas have heads but no tails. Ultimately, how is it? "The imperial decree from the West is strict.
"I shall take my leave; long life and prosperity to you."
Gao Feng said, "Mañjuśrī knows it, but Kāśyapa does not; Kāśyapa knows it, but Mañjuśrī does not.

Setting aside for a moment the fact that each does not know the other's, among these hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions of Mañjuśrīs, which one ultimately is the true Mañjuśrī?"
Tianning Qisong said: "Kāśyapa was far from being a great man. Do not speak of hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, or millions of Mañjuśrīs;

even if it were hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, or millions of World-Honored Ones, he would have struck them with a single blow and expelled them—only then would one see a true master. Have you not heard it said:
'Under the blow of the staff is the patience of non-arising; when facing the critical moment, the teacher is not seen'?"
The *Longchi chuan* says: "If I were Kāśyapa, I would first have to expel this 'yellow-faced old fellow. Why?
For one who comes to speak of right and wrong is precisely a person of right and wrong."
Gushan Xian said: "Although Mañjuśrī gained the upper hand, how could he avoid increasing his own ugliness?
Why did he not silently accept being expelled at that time, leaving Kāśyapa to search for him in vain for thirty years?"
Baoshou newly says: Where Mañjuśrī acts, Kāśyapa does not know; where Kāśyapa acts, Mañjuśrī does not recognize.
Only the Yellow-Faced Old Man has the manifest and the hidden, the provisional and the real. How can this be seen?
Clenching his teeth, he sealed the ear of Yongchi; shedding tears, he executed Dinggong.
Huìyún said: "Although the Great and Small World-Honored Ones were skilled at untangling the entanglements of these two great beings, how could they avoid being ridiculed by others?
Why? Because failing to sever what ought to be severed, one instead invites chaos."

Chongxian Qiyun said: "Mañjuśrī spent the summer retreats in three places; he pointed his head directly toward the most bustling spot. When Kāśyapa struck the gavel intending to expel him, he sided with principle rather than kin.
The World-Honored One knew in his heart that a few could not withstand the many, which resulted in the golden-colored dhūta having no place to land for the gavel to this day.
If one were under the gate of the patch-robed monks, they would know only to exhaust [all possibilities]."
“Dharma! What does it matter if there are no people?
Shitai Ren said, “Mañjuśrī spending the summer retreats in three places was also failing to maintain his own station.
Kāśyapa striking the gavel was very much like catching the wind or grasping a shadow. When the World-Honored One said, “Which Mañjuśrī do you intend to expel? at that time—
"If I were this mountain monk, I would act according to the command. Look at where this Old Man with the Yellow Face is crouching and standing!
Baiyan Fu said: "The venerable elders of all quarters all claim that the Venerable One was unable to act according to the command. Thus it led to...
This concludes the passing over. Little do people realize that at that time he had no response; there was a thorn within the soft mud, a matter of great consequence.
Those with eyes upon the crown of their heads should not say that the Venerable One failed to uphold the command.
Baofeng Bian said: "The venerable masters of past and present all claim that Kāśyapa held fast at the critical ford and Mañjuśrī cut off the ten directions.
Looking at it from Baofeng’s perspective, this was precisely letting one pass. He further said: 'Dangerous!'"
The World-Honored One, because Mañjuśrī had arrived at the assembly of all Buddhas, encountered the Buddhas each returning to their own lands.
Only a single woman remained near the World-Honored One’s seat, having entered into samādhi. Mañjuśrī said, “How is it that this woman has been able to approach the Buddha’s seat?
The World-Honored One said, “Simply awaken this woman from her samādhi; you may ask her yourself. Thereupon, Mañjuśrī...

He circumambulated the woman three times and snapped his fingers once; yet, even when he exerted his supernatural powers as far as the Brahma Heaven, he was utterly unable to release her from her meditative absorption.
The World-Honored One said, "Even if hundreds of thousands of Mañjuśrīs were to attempt it, they likewise could not release this woman from her absorption."
Below, past lands as numerous as the sands of forty-two Ganges Rivers, there was the Bodhisattva Māmaprabhā, who was indeed able to bring her out.
In an instant, Māmaprabhā surged forth from the earth, prostrated before the World-Honored One, and the World-Honored One commanded her to release the woman from her concentration.
Māmaprabhā went before the woman and snapped her fingers once; the woman then emerged from her concentration.
Cuiyan Zhi said: "A monk goes to stay overnight in a temple; a thief strikes when the household is unprepared.
Wuyun Feng said: "Not only can Mañjuśrī not emerge from this samādhi, I fear that even the Tathāgata could not emerge from it."
Cuiyan Zhen asked a monk, "Mañjuśrī is the teacher of the seven Buddhas;
why was he unable to bring the woman out of her samādhi? Wangming came from below; why was it he who could bring the woman out of her samādhi?
No one was able to respond. Only Ying of Shaowu, when asked, pinched his knee with his hand and departed. Zhen [said], "Excellent!"
He laughed and said, "The fellow who sells spoons and chopsticks has not yet appeared.
Tiantong Jue said, "Whether still or moving, it is the person himself who manipulates it. A goose feather is light, yet not light;
Mount Tai is heavy, yet not heavy. Do you know that the nostrils of old Gautama are in my hands?"
Longxiang finished presenting the public case. Holding up his staff, he said, "A single string has pierced them all.
Tiantong Wu said, "Setting aside for a moment whether one can emerge or not, what is this 'fixity'?"
Gushan Xian said: "Tiantong’s Way—whether still or moving—is for the person to manipulate;
this is so, yet it only expresses half of it. Who knows that all three were men who did not abide by their own proper lot?
The woman has not emerged from her samādhi even to this day."
Nanjian asked: "Ancients and moderns alike all say that the woman emerged from samādhi;
little do they realize that every one of this crew of fellows has ruined their own households and squandered their fortunes. Today I have thirty blows I wish for the World-Honored One to eat.
Why? If it were not for the fisherman’s guidance, how could one see the waves?"
Yuanwu Keqin said: "Some say the thread is in the hands of the woman; her taking it up or letting it go depends on her.
To judge it in such a way is like a short man crossing a deep ravine. Others say it cannot be known by wisdom (*jñāna*) nor recognized by consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Because Mañjuśrī employs wisdom and consciousness, he was unable to bring her out of samādhi. It was only when Wǎngmíng first gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment that he could do so.
Because the Bodhisattva is without wisdom and without consciousness, he is inconceivable; this is why he is able to emerge from another’s samādhi.
If you speak thus, it is like a tortoise boring through a wall. O Great Assembly, do you wish to recognize the woman? She is a jade disk that has not yet been carved.

Do you wish to recognize these two Bodhisattvas? They brought their uncut jade to the state of Chu and brought upon themselves the calamity of having their feet cut off. Do you wish to recognize the World-Honored One?
When there is nothing to do in one's leisure, one sits by the stream; the green waters and blue mountains are bright with flowers in full bloom.

Qixia Chengyun said: "If Mañjuśrī had emerged from his samādhi at that time to resolve the woman's dilemma, not only would Old Gautama’s mouth have been hung up on the wall for the rest of his life, but where in the world could the teachers of today go to find food to eat?
Nevertheless, tell me: did the woman actually ever emerge from her samādhi or not?"
Yunyan said, "This lot of fellows—with their god-like heads and ghostly faces—all deserve thirty blows of the staff.
Tianmu Lü said, "These four fellows were indispensable at the assembly on Vulture Peak; yet if they had reached Baoshou, not a single one would have been tolerated.
Why? Because here, do you think you can distinguish between those who enter and those who stay? (He gave a shout.)
One shout.
Baeryam Pu said: "Whether you can emerge or cannot emerge, you must all have a share of being struck with an iron staff.
As for Lady Gautami, let her pass with one stroke. Why? If one were to exhaust the Dharma, I fear there would be no people left."
The World-Honored One saw Mañjuśrī standing outside the gate and said, "Mañjuśrī, Mañjuśrī, why do you not enter the gate?
Mañjuśrī replied, "I do not see a single dharma outside the gate; how can you instruct me to enter?"
Baoci then questioned him, saying, "Is this a statement made outside the gate, or a statement made inside the gate?
Guishan Zhe, acting on behalf of the World-Honored One, uttered these words: "I am not your equal."
Huanglong Xin said: "When Mañjuśrī speaks thus, one may enter the gate or not enter the gate;
if one can discern this, ice melts and tiles shatter.
Wanfeng Zang said: "In every case, it is separated by a single board."
Chongxian Qi said: "The World-Honored One cannot emerge from within his own gate; Mañjuśrī cannot exit from within his own body.
If one looks closely, they are all like Xu Liu carrying a single plank."
While the World-Honored One was seated beneath a nyagrodha tree, two merchants asked him, "Did you see a carriage pass by?
He replied, "I did not see it. "Did you hear it? He replied, "I did not hear it. "Were you in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*)?

He replied, "I was not in meditative concentration. "Were you asleep? He replied, "I was not asleep. "Did you go elsewhere? He replied, "I did not go anywhere else. Thereupon, the merchants sighed in admiration.
He said, "Excellent! World-Honored One, you were awake yet did not see me. He then presented two pieces of white cotton cloth.
Tian Tongwu asked: "The merchant questioned thus, and the World-Honored One answered thus.
Where exactly was it that the merchant saw the World-Honored One being awake yet not seeing him?"
Daiyu Penglun said: "The Great Master of the Three Realms was pushed by merchants into a pit of rotten mud three hundred *zhang* deep;
to this day he cannot rise.
When the World-Honored One was offered music by the Gandharva King, at that moment the mountains, rivers, and great earth all became the sound of the lute. Kāśyapa...
The leaves began to dance as they rose. The King asked, "Kāśyapa, are you not indeed an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted? How can there still be residual habits?
The World-Honored One replied, "In truth, there are no residual habits. Do not slander the Dharma. The King then stroked the lute three times more.
Kāśyapa also performed a dance three times. The King said, "Did Kāśyapa not perform a dance? The World-Honored One said, "In truth, he never performed a dance.
The King said, "How could the World-Honored One speak falsely? The World-Honored One said, "It is no falsehood.
When you strum the lute, the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all wood and stone become the sound of the lute—is this not so? The King said, "It is. The World-Honored One said:
Kāśyapa was also like this; he truly never performed a dance. When the King thus came to believe and accept this, Heyin of Heishan asked Master Xiushan:
"When the Gandharva King plays music, it causes Mount Sumeru to tremble and the waters of the ocean to surge.
Kāśyapa performs a dance—how do you understand this? Heyin said: "Kāśyapa has passed away."
Shi once said, "A musician has come; his habitual tendencies have not yet been eliminated. Xiu asked, "What about when Mount Sumeru towers high and the waters of the sea surge with waves?
Yan replied, "He has departed. Fayen commented on Yan's response, saying, "That is precisely his habitual tendency."
Huanji said to Ji: "Some say that the World-Honored One used medicine to remove illness, while Chengyuan used illness to remove medicine.
Even in a dream, one has not yet seen the Gandharva King."
Huangbo Qi said: "When the Gandharva King performs music, Kāśyapa rises to dance. Being from the same pit, there is no difference in the soil;
yet he suspects that there are residual habits remaining, comparing himself to others. Gautama has created all this entanglement. Thereupon, the King believed and accepted it.

This was not a slight matter of neglect. Had I been this mountain monk, when asked why Kāśyapa—an Arhat whose outflows were already exhausted—still had residual habits, I would not have simply let it pass;
I would have risen to my feet in dance. Not only would I have used a wedge to drive out a wedge, but I would have caused the Gandharva King to fall into endless cycles of doubt and confusion.
Baiyan Fu said: "Everyone says that the Gandharva King had his eyes swapped out by the golden-colored dhūta;
little do they realize that the Yellow-faced Gautama had his eyes swapped out by the Gandharva King even more thoroughly."

The World-Honored One was preaching the Mahāsannipāta Sūtra in the sixth heaven. He commanded all the fierce and malevolent ghosts and spirits from other lands, this world, the human realm, and the heavens to assemble;
they were to receive the Buddha’s entrustment to protect and uphold the True Dharma.

Should there be any who did not attend, the Four Heavenly Kings would pursue them with flying wheels of glowing iron to force their gathering. Once the assembly had gathered, there was none [who did not comply].
Those who did not comply with the Buddha’s command each made a great vow to protect the True Dharma. Only one Māra king said to the World-Honored One:
"Gautama, I shall wait until all sentient beings have attained Buddhahood, until the realm of sentient beings is emptied and the very name 'sentient being' no longer exists;
only then will I resolve to attain Bodhicitta."
Jianfu Huiyun said: "To remain unchanging in the face of peril is the mark of a true great man.
You worthy ones, how can you provide a turning word to give the Yellow-Faced Old Man some breath? Ordinary spiritual powers, wondrous functions, wisdom, and eloquence are all of no use here.
Throughout the entire land of Jambudvīpa, there is no one who does not love the Buddha; yet, when it comes to this point—"
"What is the Buddha? What is Māra? Is there anyone who can distinguish them? After a long silence, he said, "If you wish to recognize Māra, it is when you open your eyes and see light.
If you wish to recognize the Buddha, it is when you close your eyes and see darkness.
Then, striking the ground once with his staff, he said, "In a single stroke, I have pierced through the nostrils of both."
Nantang Jing said: "At that time, had I been the World-Honored One, I would have said to him: 'O Great Assembly, the Demon King has already awakened the aspiration;
you should abide in this manner. Otherwise, I would have said: 'What do you call a sentient being?'"
Just as he was about to open his mouth, [Zhaozhou] gave him a red-hot iron wheel.
Jingshan Hongdao said: "The old fellow Tianyi’s critique is truly extraordinary; yet, how regrettable that he split the matter into two parts.
Had he simply desisted at the point where one asks, 'What is Buddha? What is Mara? it would have been sufficient."
People are suspicious and attached to this. Yet [the Master] says, "With eyes open one sees light; with eyes closed one sees darkness"—this is no small amount of clumsiness.
He further says, "Demons and Buddhas—the staff pierces their nostrils all at once! This is like adding frost to snow.
Miaoxi, however, speaks a substitute phrase on behalf of the Yellow-Faced Old Man: he waits for that Demon King to say, "The realm of sentient beings is empty."
"I did not give rise to the bodhicitta because there is no such thing as the name 'sentient being. I was merely saying to him, 'I nearly mistook you for a Mara-king.
These words contain two points of defeat (*parājayasthāna*). If one can examine them thoroughly and discern them, I grant that you possess the eye of a patch-robed monk (*bhikṣu*).
Dongchan Guo said: "How strange! In shallow grass, one stumbles upon a great tiger; it bites people as soon as it reaches their doors and houses.

It is a pity that he let it go at that time. If I were the World-Honored One, when it was said that 'the realm of sentient beings is empty and there is no name for a sentient being,' I would have immediately awakened the bodhicitta. All it would take was to say: 'Carrying a wooden board.'"
Han, it is not merely that his throat is choked; he is also taught such that he cannot even move.
Nevertheless, though acquaintances may fill the world, how many can truly know one’s heart?
Tianning Qisong said: "The marsh is so vast it conceals the mountains; the principle is such that it can subdue the leopard. What need is there for these two great elders to say more?
At that time, one simply needed to tell him: "Māra, Māra! Which of these do you recognize as the bodhicitta?"

Do you still recognize it? Even if all sentient beings were to attain Buddhahood until the realm of sentient beings was emptied and the very name "sentient being" ceased to exist, I would not grant you permission to give rise to the bodhicitta; you shall surely be forced to surrender with folded hands.
Longchi Chuanzheng said: "Now tell me, does this Demon King take refuge in the Buddha’s words, or does he not take refuge in the Buddha’s words?
Yunmen Xin said: "Within the Demon King’s words there is resonance; his protection of the Dharma is complete."
Baoneng Xiu said: "The World-Honored One’s silence was replete with a hundred flavors;

Tianyi Daohui, though the most extraordinary among the extraordinary, when scrutinized, cannot avoid failing to distinguish gold from sand or beans from wheat—like a small child eating a plum, hastily biting into the red flesh.
For the sake of the World-Honored One, Daxiong dares to utter a word: 'Tsk! Man!'"
"Son, you have already resolved upon Bodhicitta. If anyone were to deliberate or question this, give them a red-hot iron wheel.
Chongxian Qi said, "The Old Man with the Yellow Face can speak but cannot practice.

At that time, he waited until he said, 'I shall only resolve upon Bodhicitta when the realm of sentient beings is empty and the very name of a sentient being no longer exists. Why did he not [act accordingly]?"
"If you say I am not your equal, I shall certainly bow my head and surrender. Why? Have you not heard it said:
'Under heavy rewards, there are bound to be brave men'?
Putuo Wuo said, "But tell me, what kind of eyes does this Mara possess that he dares speak in such a manner?"
Baiyan Fu said: "This Demon King is very much like a golden-scaled fish that has passed through the net; he shakes his head and wags his tail amidst a thousand layers of waves.
The World-Honored One may truly be said to have cast his hook not in vain. However, I must ask this Demon King:
since the realm of sentient beings is empty and there are no names for sentient beings, from where do you emerge?"
Regarding "Bodhicitta": as soon as the other was about to open his mouth, [Linji] struck him with the staff and drove him out.
Longyuan Fachun remarked, "The World-Honored One had his tongue cut off by the Mara King; Longyuan, seeing this injustice on the road, wishes to clear his master's grievance.
As soon as [the student] was about to speak thus, [Longyuan] said, "I know you! If one hesitates for even a moment, one will not be able to respond.
"Splitting the spine, he struck with the staff.

Youke Xuan said, "The Great Assemblage Māra was small-souled and thin-hearted; at that time, he should have immediately overturned the Flower King’s throne and shouted to disperse the assembly of humans and devas.
This would not have failed to leave people in a state of doubt. Yet he instead said, 'Wait until the realm of sentient beings...'"
"Since there are no sentient beings and no names for them in emptiness, I have then resolved to attain enlightenment. This is truly "tying up one's topknot and rushing to the yamen";
it deserves twenty strokes with a broom.
Changshan Liang said, "World-Honored One, had you not possessed the mechanism of wielding authority beyond the threshold, you would have nearly been seized by the Demon King."
"Delusion and confusion, Part One. Nevertheless, if there were someone here who did not wish to resolve to attain Bodhicitta, one might grant that they possess a single eye.
Wanshou Lang said: "The old Gautama has a vanguard but no rear guard. At that time, he waited for [the Buddha] to say, "I wait..."
"The realm of sentient beings is empty; there are no such things as names for sentient beings," and so forth.
[The Buddha] then gave him a hot iron wheel, lest he seek refuge upon pure, white ground. Is there anyone here who can act as the master over the Demon King?
Holding up his staff, he said, "Look, look, everyone! The Four Heavenly Kings are flying hot iron wheels here!
With a whirlwind motion of his staff, he scattered them.
